title: The Tall Glass and the Wide Glass
text:
In Geneva in the 1930s and 1940s, the Swiss psychologist Jean Piaget and his collaborator Alina Szeminska sat with children of different ages and presented them with deceptively simple puzzles. In the best known, a child watched as two identical glasses were filled with the same amount of liquid. The child agreed that both held the same.

Then, in front of the child, the researcher poured the liquid from one glass into a taller, thinner one, and asked: is there the same amount to drink in both, or does one have more? Most children of four or five said the tall glass now had more, because the liquid came up higher. Some said it had less, because it was thinner. The pouring had happened right before their eyes, yet the appearance won.

Older children, usually from around six or seven, answered differently and with confidence: it is the same, because nothing was added or taken away, or because it is taller but thinner, or because you could pour it back. Piaget called this understanding conservation and found the same pattern with rows of counters spread out or pushed together, and with balls of clay rolled into sausages.

Piaget concluded that young children do not simply know less than adults; they reason in a different way.
lesson: When a child gives an answer that seems silly, they may be reasoning in a different way rather than not trying. Ask how they see it before correcting them.
source: Piaget, J., and Szeminska, A. (1941). La genese du nombre chez l'enfant. Neuchatel: Delachaux et Niestle. English translation: The Child's Conception of Number (1952).
caveat: Later researchers found that young children often succeed when the task is made more natural or the questions less confusing, so Piaget probably underestimated what they can understand.
